newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welcomes Kabila election pledge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welcomes Kabila election pledge.

text.p: The United States welcomed a pledge on Thursday by President Laurent Kabila to hold elections in the Democratic Republic of Congo in April 1999, saying a two-year transition period seemed reasonable.
"We believe this is a positive step" by Kabila, whose forces overthrew President Mobutu Sese Seko earlier this month, State Department spokesman John Dinger said.

"We have said that we hope that elections are held sooner rather than later. We have to understand that Congo confronts real and severe problems...a two-year period in that context does not seem unreasonable to us," Dinger told reporters.

Kabila, who took office on Thursday as president, said in an address to the nation that he was in no hurry to hold elections as the "crumbling and shattered state", formerly known as Zaire, needed to be organised first.

Dinger welcomed Kabila's establishment of a pre-election timetable, including the drafting of a new constitution that would be put to an elected constitutional assembly and finally to the people in a referendum in December 1998.
Dinger declined direct comment on the sweeping powers Kabila has assigned himself but said he hoped all parties and factions would be given a voice during the transition period.
He added that Washington would be "monitoring the situation closely" to see that Kabila lived up to his promises to establish democracy in Congo.
Dinger also reiterated U.S. concern at Kabila's failure so far to let the international community investigate reports of massacres in areas of eastern Congo controlled by his troops.
"Today we want to urgently call on President Kabila to grant access to the sites of reported massacres and also access to refugees who may still be in Congo," he said.
